name: Assyria
summary: A Mesopotamian kingdom from the city of Assur that became the first great military superpower. At its height it ruled from Egypt to Iran.

location.value: Northern Mesopotamia, on the Tigris, ruled from Assur, later Nimrud and Nineveh.

terrain.value: Rain-fed farmland and hills along the upper Tigris.

climate.value: Some research links late drought to the empire’s collapse.

resources.value: Grain from rain-fed farms; metals, horses and timber came by trade or tribute.

disasters.value: Droughts and river floods; a long drought may have weakened Assyria before its fall.

population.value: No reliable estimate. Nineveh was among the largest cities of its time.

urbanisation.value: Capitals moved from Assur to Nimrud (879 BCE), Dur-Sharrukin (706 BCE) and Nineveh (705 BCE).

disease.value: Epidemics are mentioned in the 8th century BCE.

migration.value: Mass deportations moved hundreds of thousands of people around the empire.

economicBase.value: Agriculture, tribute from conquered lands, and earlier long-distance trade.

tradeRoutes.value: Old Assyrian merchants traded tin and textiles to Kanesh in Anatolia (the Kültepe tablets).

wealth.value: No estimate is possible for this period.

moneyAndTax.value: Silver by weight; tribute and taxes collected from provinces.

inequality.value: King and nobles at the top; deportees and slaves at the bottom.

governmentType.value: Monarchy. The king was the representative of the god Ashur.

keyRulers.value: Shamshi-Adad I, Ashur-uballit I, Tiglath-Pileser III (745–727 BCE), Sargon II, Sennacherib (705–681 BCE), Ashurbanipal (669–631 BCE).

succession.value: Hereditary, but often contested, sometimes through murder (Sennacherib was killed by his sons).

institutions.value: Provinces under governors, a royal road and postal system, and the first large libraries.

stability.value: Repeated revolts in Babylon and a civil war between Ashurbanipal and his brother (652–648 BCE).

eliteConflict.value: Succession conflicts, including the murder of Sennacherib.

armyAndTech.value: The strongest army of its time: iron weapons, cavalry, chariots, siege engines and a professional standing army.

majorWars.value: Conquest of the Kingdom of Israel (722 BCE), Babylon (729 BCE), and Egypt (671 BCE).

territoryChange.value: At its height it ruled from Egypt to western Iran.

alliancesRivals.value: Rivals: Babylon, Elam, Urartu, Egypt and the Medes.

inventions.value: Large-scale use of iron weapons, organised siege warfare, and early libraries.

scienceEducation.value: The Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, with tens of thousands of clay tablets.

openness.value: Adopted Babylonian learning; Aramaic spread as a common language.

communicationTransport.value: A royal road system with relay stations carried messages quickly; horses, chariots and river rafts on inflated skins.

religion.value: Mesopotamian religion, centred on the god Ashur.

languageWriting.value: Akkadian (Assyrian dialect) in cuneiform, and later Aramaic.

artsArchitecture.value: Palace relief carvings (lion hunts, sieges) and colossal winged bulls (lamassu).

socialStructure.value: King, nobles, priests, scribes, soldiers, farmers, deportees and slaves.

sharedIdentity.value: Loyalty to the king and to the god Ashur, after whom the land and capital were named.

dailyLife.value: Mud-brick houses in cities like Nineveh; barley, dates, sesame oil and beer; officials wore fringed wool robes.

neighbours.value: Babylon, Elam, Urartu, Egypt, the Medes, and the kingdoms of Israel and Judah.

ideasReligions.value: Its imperial model was copied by Babylon and Persia.

colonisation.value: Deported conquered populations, including the Israelites of the northern kingdom.

riseSignals.value: Ashur-uballit I made Assyria a great power; Tiglath-Pileser III reorganised the army.

declineSignals.value: Civil war, Babylonian revolt (626 BCE), and the alliance of Babylonians, Medes and Scythians.

outcome.value: Nineveh fell in 612 BCE; the last king lost Harran in 609 BCE. Successors: Neo-Babylonian and Median empires.
outcome.source: Wikipedia: Assyria (checked 6 Nov 2026); Britannica: Assyria (checked 9 Nov 2026)

sources.value: Royal annals, palace reliefs, letters and the Library of Ashurbanipal. Checked against Wikipedia (“Assyria”).

overallCertainty.value: Good for the Neo-Assyrian period; earlier dates are approximate. Start date differs by definition: this app starts with the city-state of Ashur in the Old Assyrian period (c. 2025 BCE, following Wikipedia), while Britannica (checked 9 Nov 2026) says Assyria was dependent on Babylonia and Mitanni for most of the 2nd millennium BCE and became an independent state in the 14th century BCE. Britannica agrees on the end (destroyed by a Chaldean–Median coalition in 612–609 BCE) and counts Tiglath-Pileser III, Sargon II, Sennacherib and Esarhaddon among the kings at its height, with Ashurbanipal the last great ruler.
overallCertainty.source: Wikipedia: Assyria (checked 6 Nov 2026); Britannica: Assyria (checked 9 Nov 2026)

knownFor.label: Lamassu winged bulls
knownFor.note: Colossal human-headed winged bulls guarding palace gates.

knownFor.label: Library of Ashurbanipal
knownFor.note: A royal library of clay tablets at Nineveh that preserved the Epic of Gilgamesh.

knownFor.label: Iron weapons & siege engines
knownFor.note: A professional army with iron weapons, battering rams and siege towers.

knownFor.label: Palace relief carvings
knownFor.note: Stone panels showing lion hunts and sieges.
